Stated Claim / Post Context:
Aussie politician unleashes after paying $12.40 for just a loaf of white bread and milk: 'That barely feeds a couple of kids'

A politican has slammed the price of milk and other basic every day needs - blaming the Albanese government for driving inflation.

Actual Article Body:
By NICHOLAS COMINO, POLITICAL REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  12:04 AEST, 1 October 2026   |  Updated:  12:26 AEST, 1 October 2026

Liberal frontbencher Melissa McIntosh unleashed at the Albanese government after paying $12.40 for just two litres of milk and a loaf of bread,

Speaking to Patricia Karvelas on ABC's Afternoon Briefing on Wednesday, McIntosh said everyday Australians were struggling to keep up with soaring living costs, warning that Labor's spending policies were helping drive inflation.

'I came by the shops and a two-litre bottle of milk and a loaf of white bread cost $12.40, and that barely feeds a couple of kids for a couple of hours,' she said, holding up the items during the interview.

'This is what people are paying for milk and bread, let alone what they're paying for their mortgages and their rents to keep a roof over their families' heads.'

McIntosh blamed the Albanese Government for the country's economic difficulties, accusing Labor of refusing to rein in spending despite persistent inflation.

'We are in this position because of this government, high inflation, and they just won't back down on their homegrown expenditure,' she said.

She also took aim at Treasurer Jim Chalmers, accusing him of deflecting responsibility for inflation by pointing to international events.

'I couldn't believe Jim Chalmers today,' McIntosh said.

Melissa McIntosh (pictured) said Jim Chalmers was 'lying' about why inflation was rising

She revealed the hefty price for the common staple during an interview with ABC star Patricia Karvelas

'If it was a drinking game and Australians had a drink every time he tried to blame the war in the Middle East, the pubs would have run dry.

'He is lying when he is saying this is all about the war in the Middle East. There's nothing to see here.'

McIntosh argued government spending had become a key driver of inflationary pressures, highlighting the size of the public sector's contribution to the economy and the nation's debt burden.

'When you've got nearly 28 per cent of GDP coming from government spending, of course inflation is going to be high,' she said.

'We've got $1 trillion of debt and when you've got $1 trillion of debt, you're paying off that debt. It's like having a bad credit card.

'$33 billion a year is just paying off that debt. Imagine the hospital funding. Imagine the infrastructure that could be built.'

Pressed on whether the Coalition would need to find savings, including rising costs tied to indexed payments, through cuts to social services, McIntosh hit back.

'We're not looking to cut support,' she said.

Jim Chalmers (pictured) rejected claims government spending was a main driver of inflation

How has the rising cost of basic groceries affected your family’s daily life and priorities?

'I'm in Penrith in western Sydney where people are doing it really tough right now and I'm hearing more and more people are going onto the social welfare system, not because they want to, but because they need to.'

Instead, she said governments should focus on making sure taxpayer money delivered real results rather than just increasing spending.

'For too long, success has been judged on the amount of money that is being thrown at programs,'  McIntosh said.

'We need to ensure that the money is having a positive impact on people's lives.

'I don't want to see the line-ups at the food banks I'm seeing now where the working homeless are making a decision between having a roof over their heads, paying the bills for having that roof over their heads, or feeding their families,' she said.

The government has pushed back on claims its spending is driving inflation, with Chalmers arguing global factors, including conflict in the Middle East, remain a key source of price pressures through higher oil costs.

'Public demand growth has slowed considerably,' Chalmers said on Thursday.

'In fact, it came in even lower in the budget numbers we released on Monday than what we were anticip
